html:
The capital of the Abbasid caliphate, founded in 762 by the caliph al-Mansur on the Tigris in what is now Iraq. He called it Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, and built it as a round city with circular walls, four gates and his palace and mosque at the centre.

The site lay near the old Sasanian capital Ctesiphon, where the Tigris and Euphrates run close together and trade routes met. It replaced Damascus, the capital of the Umayyads. Within decades Baghdad spread far beyond the round walls and became one of the largest cities in the world, perhaps the largest, in the 9th and 10th centuries.

Under Harun al-Rashid and his sons it was the centre of Islamic learning and trade. Paper mills, booksellers and the House of Wisdom fed the translation of Greek science, and Indian numerals arrived here. The tales of the Thousand and One Nights remember its splendour. As the caliphs lost real power, others ruled in their name. The Mongol sack of 1258 ended the caliphate and wrecked the city.
